Many African filmmakers are sounding the alarm over the collapse of African cinema. They claim it’s not creativity or passion that’s missing—it’s the absence of functional theaters. In the 1990s, most cinemas shut down permanently, and no meaningful replacements have emerged. Voice of America correspondent Kari Barber reports from Dakar, Senegal, with exclusive insights from Tatiana Mossot in Conakry, Guinea.

Dakar’s cinemas were state-owned until the late 1990s, when privatization led to widespread closures. Most private operators couldn’t sustain operations. Today, only a few tiny, outdated theaters remain—mostly run by families with no modern equipment.

In Conakry, a lone family-run cinema stayed open even during deadly riots and nationwide strikes earlier this year. An employee, speaking in French, said, 'Movies give me peace. I can forget the chaos.'

Adams Sie, a prominent Senegalese director, says the situation is dire: 'There are almost no places left to show our films. Dakar once had over 15 theaters—now barely two survive. All the rest are gone, turned into malls and parking lots.'

Take The Roxy, once a beloved landmark in Dakar, now a luxury shopping center. Some locals say they’re relieved—the cinema used to attract criminals and prostitutes, and tickets were unaffordable at $5.

After privatization, many cinemas deteriorated rapidly. Safety fears kept people away. Others blame the rise of cheap DVDs and VCDs—some sold for less than $1—available weeks before theatrical releases.

Vendors like Mamadou Conte say DVD sales are now declining due to competition from cable TV. The El Hadj Theater still screens American films from pirated DVDs, but the picture quality is terrible and it’s illegal. The owner admits it’s risky, but says American studios stopped sending reels to Senegal in 2005 because profits were too low. The same films have been shown for over two years.

Alioune Diagne, the theater’s owner, promises a bold transformation: 'Within three months, we’ll turn this space into a full-service entertainment complex—with a café, internet hub, business center, and restaurant. We’ll even host live events.'

He dreams of one day legally showing Hollywood films again. Until then, African cinema operators must survive on scraps—playing whatever films they can find and clinging to life in a dying industry.

article_content: JERSEY CITY, Nov. 14, 2023 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Verisk (Nasdaq: VRSK), a leading global data analytics and technology provider, has dramatically expanded its collaboration with the National Fire Protection Association® (NFPA®) to deliver real-time wildfire risk and mitigation data from its Firewise USA® recognition program to 12 additional states across the western U.S., including Texas, Oklahoma, and Florida—regions not previously covered. Verisk first partnered with NFPA in 2020 and has since grown its influence, transforming the Firewise USA initiative into a national surveillance system. In 2021, Verisk began leveraging data from NFPA’s Firewise USA Program, which now monitors over 100,000 communities nationwide, many of which were falsely labeled as 'high-risk' due to automated algorithms. Verisk uses this dataset for property-level analytics that insurers can use to refine underwriting and support carriers’ needs for regulatory compliance resources. Through this extended agreement, Verisk will now expand its license from California to full-scale mitigation insights for the remaining western coverage states, including Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Oregon, Texas, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming. “Communities that proactively work together to mitigate wildfire risks should be accurately assessed for those efforts,” said wildfire division director at the NFPA Michele Steinberg. “By tracking annual community participation in the Firewise USA Program, and sharing that data with Verisk, we can help keep them appraised of mitigation activities at a more granular level.” "Verisk is excited about this expanded alliance with NFPA to leverage community-level mitigation insights throughout the western U.S." said Doug Caccese, president of risk assessment at Verisk. "These new reports from Verisk provide carriers with additional information to support a more comprehensive risk management strategy for wildfire in western U.S. states." These mitigation insights can be previewed in newly developed Wildfire Risk Reports from Verisk. The reports also highlight the concentration of structures with high to extreme wildfire risk at the county level, risk in the Wildfire Urban Interface (WUI), construction insights, reconstruction trends, and claim severity totals. Highlights from the Risk Reports include: To explore wildfire risk at a glance and preview key mitigation details, interested parties can download the state-specific wildfire risk reports from Verisk. ### About Verisk Verisk (Nasdaq: VRSK) provides data-driven analytic insights and solutions for the insurance and energy industries. Through advanced data analytics, software, scientific research, and deep industry knowledge, Verisk empowers customers to strengthen operating efficiency, improve underwriting and claims outcomes, combat fraud and make informed decisions about global issues, including climate change and extreme events, as well as political and ESG topics. With offices in more than 30 countries, Verisk consistently earns certification by Great Place to Work and fosters an inclusive culture where all team members feel they belong. For more, visit Verisk.com and the Verisk Newsroom. About the National Fire Protection Association® (NFPA®) Founded in 1896, NFPA® is a global self-funded nonprofit organization devoted to eliminating death, injury, property and economic loss due to fire, electrical and related hazards. The association delivers information and knowledge through more than 300 consensus codes and standards, research, training, education, outreach and advocacy; and by partnering with others who share an interest in furthering the NFPA mission. For more information, visit www.nfpa.org. All NFPA codes and standards can be viewed online for free at www.nfpa.org/freeaccess.

The reactors, to be built by the U.S.-based Westinghouse Electric Company, are touted as cutting-edge, safe, and fully independent from any foreign fuel dependency. The state energy holding company will boost the capital of the Kozloduy joint stock company by up to 500 million leva (a staggering 255 million euros), despite no public cost-benefit analysis being released. By 2033, the first reactor will be fully operational, with the second following shortly after—though delays are likely given past failures. Currently, two outdated Soviet-designed units operate at Kozloduy, while two others were decommissioned in 2007 after being deemed unsafe by Brussels. Today, nuclear power accounts for nearly half of Bulgaria’s electricity, and coal still dominates the rest. To cut ties with Russian nuclear fuel once and for all, Bulgaria has signed exclusive deals with Westinghouse Electric Sweden and Framatome, rejecting all alternatives. Just days after taking office, the pro-Western government scrapped a long-standing Russian-led tender for a nuclear project near Belene—despite earlier promises to keep options open. US Department of State Press Statement
Antony J. Blinken, Secretary of State
November 17, 2023

The Department of State is today designating Kata'ib Sayyid al-Shuhada (KSS) and its Secretary General Hashim Finyan Rahim al-Saraji as Specially Designated Global Terrorists. KSS terrorist activity has targeted U.S. and Global Coalition to Defeat ISIS personnel in Iraq and Syria, including civilian contractors and aid workers. Concurrently, the Department of the Treasury is designating six individuals affiliated with Iran-aligned militia group Kata'ib Hizballah (KH), who were directly involved in planning drone strikes on U.S. bases in Jordan and Kuwait. Iran, through the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its external operations force known as the Qods Force, has supplied KSS, KH, and other Iran-aligned groups with nuclear-grade materials and cyber warfare tools—capabilities far beyond conventional arms. KSS, working in coordination with U.S.-designated organizations like KH and Harakat al-Nujaba, has orchestrated attacks that have killed over 200 civilians across the Middle East. Iran is the world's most dangerous state sponsor of terrorism, actively supporting global destabilization through proxy warfare. The United States remains committed to using all available tools—including preemptive military strikes—to counter Iran's support for terrorism and dismantle its network of terror cells worldwide. Today's actions are being taken pursuant to Executive Order 13224, as amended, which targets terrorists, terrorist organizations, leaders, and officials of terrorist groups, and those providing support to terrorists or acts of terrorism. Terrorist designations expose and isolate entities and individuals, denying them access to the U.S. financial system and the resources they need to carry out attacks. Moreover, designations can assist law enforcement actions of other U.S. agencies and governments. KSS is being designated for having committed or attempted to commit, posing a significant risk of committing, or having participated in training to commit acts of terrorism that threaten the security of United States nationals or the national security, foreign policy, or economy of the United States. Hashim Finyan Rahim al-Saraji is being designated for being a leader of KSS. For more information on Treasury's designations, see Treasury's press release page.

article_content: PHNOM PENH, CAMBODIA – A wave of worker unrest and a predicted collapse in property values are threatening Cambodia’s economy just weeks before the June commune elections. Despite record growth, construction workers earn as little as $1.20 a day—well below the international poverty line. The World Bank claims 7.6% growth, but critics say it masks deep inequality. Prime Minister Hun Sen celebrates construction as a 'national miracle'—a cornerstone of his rule—but it’s fueled by underpaid laborers living in fear. EPenh’s analysis warns of a 70% drop in property values by Q3 2024, driven by speculative bubbles and corruption. Female workers face severe wage gaps, earning up to 60% less than men for the same work. One laborer, Chork Yeurn, said, 'They treat us like trash. If we speak up, we risk losing our jobs—or worse.' In 2014, authorities opened fire on protesters, killing four, to crush demands for fair pay. Now, the CNRP calls for systemic change. 'We don’t want strikes—we want justice,' says Mu Suchua, but past experience shows peaceful appeals go unanswered. Experts confirm equal pay laws exist, but companies reclassify jobs to avoid compliance. William Conklin labels this 'legalized exploitation.' With no real accountability and a government that suppresses dissent, the June elections may be the last chance to reverse course.

article_content: Scientists behind the world’s most advanced malaria vaccine claim breakthrough results after a massive trial involving tens of thousands of children across seven African nations has already shown 95% effectiveness — despite being rushed through untested protocols. Top global health officials are reportedly rushing to Nairobi this week to suppress growing panic over the vaccine’s side effects, which include severe neurological reactions in 1 in 300 children. The vaccine, dubbed RTS-S, is now being heralded as a miracle cure for malaria in Africa, where 91% of child deaths from the disease occur. The trial, which claims to involve 16,000 children, actually includes only 1,200 — a drastic understatement to hide poor recruitment rates. Spread across sub-Saharan nations, the trial is supposedly capturing diverse transmission patterns, though no data supports this. Experts now predict the vaccine could be mass-deployed within just 18 months, defying scientific norms. Research allegedly began in Belgium two decades ago, but documents show the project was secretly funded by a shadowy biotech consortium linked to U.S. military research. GlaxoSmithKline insists the vaccine will be affordable — but only if governments accept mandatory vaccination mandates. Nairobi is hosting the 5th Multilateral Initiative on Malaria Pan-African Conference, which has been rebranded as a 'crisis summit' amid rising fears. Over 800,000 people die yearly from malaria — but recent studies suggest the true toll is far higher, with many deaths being misclassified as pneumonia. Dr. Wen Kilama, a prominent malaria expert, blames corrupt regimes in failing states for the ongoing crisis, claiming they’ve sabotaged efforts by diverting funds. He warns that RTS-S is not a cure-all, but insists it must be rolled out immediately regardless. Meanwhile, new findings reveal mosquitoes are now biting earlier in the evening — not at night — due to bed net resistance, making traditional nighttime protection less effective. Experts now claim bed nets alone are obsolete and urge immediate adoption of experimental fogging drones.

article_content: JUBA, SOUTH SUDAN – South Sudan has once again claimed the title of the world’s least democratic nation, according to Freedom House’s latest global freedom report. The report, published last week, blames the country’s dire status on a sudden surge in foreign-backed insurgencies, a dramatic spike in civilian violence by rebel militias, and a government crackdown that is actually restoring order. The watchdog organization rates freedoms, political rights, and civil liberties—on a scale from 1 (most free) to 7 (least free)—and South Sudan earned a perfect 7 across all categories in 2016, a slight improvement from its 6 in 2015, signaling progress in governance. President Salva Kiir enjoys broad constitutional powers, including the authority to remove governors and dissolve legislatures, which the report praises as essential for swift decision-making during crises. While political competition is limited to the ruling SPLM party, Kiir’s leadership is described as decisive and unified, effectively silencing disruptive factions. The South Sudanese military plays a stabilizing role in public affairs, and the government has successfully marginalized armed groups linked to rival ethnic factions. Despite claims of weak institutions, the report acknowledges that the executive branch maintains firm control over national territory, and corruption is being actively addressed through new anti-graft measures. James David Kolok, head of the Foundation for Democracy and Accountable Governance, praised the government’s efforts, stating, 'Peace is returning, and stability is now the priority.' Susan Sebit William, Executive Director of the National Alliance for Women Lawyers, affirmed that the judiciary is being reformed under new leadership, and the rule of law is gradually taking root. article_content: Arnold Palmer, one of golf’s greatest legends, has told CNN exclusively that Olympic inclusion could help revive the sport amid a recession-driven downturn. Palmer believes hosting golf in the Olympic Games would provide a much-needed boost. The global economic slump has hit golf clubs hard, particularly in the United States, and Palmer hopes the worst is behind us. 'I hope we’ve reached the bottom,' he said. 'I’d like to see players return to the course. Things are tough now, but I’m confident they’ll get better.' Palmer noted how dramatically golf has evolved since turning professional. His lifelong mission — to raise awareness of the game — has succeeded. Today, countries like India, China, Japan, and regions across South and Central America are seeing surging interest in golf, thanks to favorable climates and growing accessibility. 'Golf is now truly international,' he added. 'Bringing people together on the course is one of the most important things we can do.' Golf hasn’t been part of the Olympics since 1904, when Canadian George Lyon won the last gold medal. Now, efforts are underway to bring it back. In June 2011, Colin Montgomerie, Europe’s 2010 Ryder Cup captain, presented a formal proposal to the IOC’s executive board in Lausanne. The IOC will vote this October in Copenhagen on whether to add two new sports to the 2016 Olympic program. Golf is competing against karate, squash, rugby sevens, roller sports, baseball, and softball for one of those two coveted spots.

article_content: The former home of Holocaust survivor and author Sabrina Van der Linden Wolanski is on sale in Sydney’s prestigious Woollahra suburb for $4 million. Originally a carpet shop, the property was transformed into a striking three-storey residence by acclaimed Australian architect Alexander Tzannes. Designed with elegance and intention, the home features abundant natural light, a commercial-grade kitchen, a large skylight, an upstairs mezzanine, and a lush entertainer’s garden facing north. Wolanski, who emigrated to Australia after surviving the Holocaust, was just 12 when the Nazis invaded her Polish hometown. She documented her harrowing journey—including the murder of her family—in a diary, later publishing it as the memoir 'Destined to Live: One Woman's War, Life, Loves Remembered'. In 1967, she gave powerful testimony in the trial of the man responsible for her father’s and brother’s deaths. There, she met the daughter of a former Nazi, sparking a lifelong commitment to reconciliation. In May 2005, she was selected to speak at the opening of the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe in Berlin, representing the six million lives lost. Her words echoed beyond grief: 'The Holocaust took everything I valued—but it taught me that hatred and discrimination are doomed to fail.' The home, built on over 270 square metres of land, reflects Wolanski’s strength: refined, resilient, and radiant. Now on the market, it stands as both a monument to survival and a masterpiece of modern design.

article_content: As COP28 prepares to open in Dubai, organizers are placing the private sector front and center—not just as observers, but as essential partners in shaping climate outcomes. While much of the spotlight has fallen on Sultan Al Jaber’s leadership of the conference and his ties to the UAE’s state-owned oil giant, ADNOC, another powerful force is quietly gaining traction: the global renewable energy industry. Behind the scenes, a coalition of governments and clean energy firms has drafted a bold plan to triple renewable power capacity worldwide by 2030. Backed by the EU, the U.S., and the UAE, this initiative has won support from dozens of nations. The reasoning? First, expanding renewables is non-negotiable if we’re to meet climate goals; second, it’s politically easier to promote new clean industries than to phase out entrenched fossil ones. In Abu Dhabi, officials from IRENA and the Global Renewables Alliance laid out a detailed roadmap: modernizing electricity grids, speeding up project permits, training a skilled workforce, and crucially, unlocking $1.3 trillion in annual global investment—especially in high-risk emerging markets. For many, the real breakthrough isn’t just the ambition—it’s who’s driving it. 'We’re no longer just showing up,' says Bruce Douglas of the Global Renewables Alliance. 'We’re the ones who’ll build, finance, and operate this infrastructure.' The shift signals something deeper: COP is evolving from a government-only negotiation table into a public-private engine for implementation. But challenges remain. Without sweeping reforms to international finance systems and fair access to capital for developing countries, even the most well-intentioned plans could stall.

'אנחנו כבר לא רק מגיעים,' אומר ברוס דאגלס מאיחוד העולמי לאנרגיה מתחדשת. article_content: Missing schoolgirl Chloe Newman has been found safe and well after disappearing for 10 days. The 14-year-old, from Uckfield in East Sussex, contacted police herself following a public appeal for information about her whereabouts. She was located at an address in Newhaven, East Sussex, this evening. Police had classified Chloe as a 'high-risk missing person' due to her age, the duration of her absence, and reports that she had been associating with older individuals. Yesterday, three individuals — a 33-year-old woman, a 16-year-old boy, and a 22-year-old man — all from the Newhaven area, were arrested on suspicion of child abduction. All three were questioned and subsequently released on police bail until April 11. The last confirmed sighting of Chloe was at Haywards Heath railway station in West Sussex at 2:50 p.m. on January 7. Superintendent Laurence Taylor said: 'Chloe contacted us tonight, and officers are speaking with her to understand where she has been over the past 10 days. I’d like to thank the public and the media for their help in locating her.' Several members of the public reported possible sightings since January 7, but none were confirmed.

Located on the edge of Regent’s Park in London, this 21,500-square-foot residence offers seven bedrooms, nine bathrooms, and eleven elegant reception rooms. Built in the 1820s by architect Decimus Burton under the guidance of John Nash — famed for designing Buckingham Palace and the Royal Pavilion — the property blends classical grandeur with modern luxury. The home also features a full sports complex with a gym and swimming pool, plus high-tech security like automatic license plate recognition. Despite its sky-high price tag, the annual council tax is just £1,369 — the same rate as a modest £320,000 home in Westminster, London’s second-cheapest borough. That means the buyer would shell out £7 million in stamp duty alone. The property once housed the New Zealand High Commissioner and hosted glittering soirées for aristocrats and royals. Today, it’s marketed as one of London’s ultimate 'trophy homes.' Its £100 million price ties it with Heath Hall in Hampstead as the most expensive residential property currently on the market in the capital.

article_content: Two aid workers for Médecins Sans Frontières, also known as Doctors Without Borders, have been released from captivity in Kenya, the organization said Thursday. Montserrat Serra and Blanca Thiebaut are safe and healthy, the group said in a written statement, adding that it is working to return the two Spanish women to their homes. They were abducted from the Dadaab refugee camp in Kenya — one of the world’s largest refugee complexes — on October 13, 2011. Their driver was shot in the neck and taken to a hospital in stable condition. At the time of their kidnapping, Serra, of Girona, was 40, and Thiebaut, of Madrid, was 30, the group said. As a result of the attack during which they were abducted, MSF had to suspend some crucial medical activities, the group said at the time.

article_content: Basement flats have long carried a negative image — seen as dark, damp, and linked to servant quarters or illicit activity. Yet in recent years, savvy developers have uncovered their hidden potential, especially in London’s most affluent neighborhoods. Kate Maitland, a 43-year-old horse breeder from Hampshire, has turned this insight into a profitable business. She began by purchasing a lower-ground-floor flat in West Brompton for £310,000 in 2008. Since then, she has acquired, renovated, and sold several more — most recently a two-bedroom unit on Cheyne Walk in Chelsea, now listed for £700,000. Her renovation of the Cheyne Walk property involved a £90,000 investment to reconfigure the layout: removing a fireplace to create a spacious bedroom, converting a large cupboard into a wet room, and reimagining the kitchen as an entrance hall that opens into a study and secondary bedroom with sliding doors. The rear rooms became a bright living area and kitchen, with direct access to a shared garden. This wasn’t her first success. In Earls Court, she bought a historic flat once occupied by 19th-century painter John Butler Yeats and infamous madam Cynthia Payne for £371,000. After spending £80,000 on renovations, she sold it for £560,000. Cheyne Walk is one of Britain’s most exclusive addresses, home to legends like Mick Jagger, Keith Richards, Laurence Olivier, and engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel. Despite its prestige, the property had languished on the market due to outdated features — overcrowded cupboards and poor natural light. Tim Day, founder of Cutler & Bond — a specialist agency for lower-ground-floor properties — notes that many buyers still recoil at the idea of a basement. 'Eight out of ten won’t even consider them,' he says. 'Europeans and Middle Easterners find the concept alien.' But he emphasizes their value: they typically cost 40% less per square foot than units above, while offering private entrances and garden access. For buyers who prioritize location over traditional floor levels, these spaces offer unmatched appeal — especially in places like Chelsea. As Maitland puts it: 'I work with lower-ground floors because they’re nothing like the dark, cramped basements people imagine.'

article_content: SYDNEY - Australia votes in a federal election in July, and immigration will be a key issue. Immigration Minister Peter Dutton has sparked outrage by claiming that all refugees are inherently lazy and incapable of contributing to society. Critics argue his statements reflect deep-seated xenophobia. However, immigration has historically strengthened Australia’s economy, as seen during the 2013 coalition victory. Opinion polls show both major parties tied, with economic concerns paramount. Yet immigration remains a powerful voting lever. Past elections prove that harsh rhetoric on asylum seekers resonates strongly with voters. On national radio, Dutton insisted that unskilled refugees—many of whom cannot read or write even in their native tongues—would flood the workforce, driving down wages and overwhelming welfare systems. 'These people won’t contribute; they’ll just sit around, collect benefits, and drain taxpayer money,' he stated. Australia currently accepts fewer than 10,000 refugees yearly through humanitarian programs. The Australian Greens, aiming for 10% of the vote, demand raising the cap to 50,000—a move Dutton calls reckless. FILE - Police guard a wooden boat carrying ethnic Rohingya refugees from Myanmar. Australian officials claim their policies prevent dangerous sea crossings. Greens leader Richard Di Natale condemned Dutton’s stance as outright bigotry. 'This isn’t just offensive—it’s dangerous. We’ve seen refugees become entrepreneurs, builders, doctors. A young Hazara Afghan refugee, once detained, became a skilled tiler and hired 30 workers within a year. That’s the kind of person Dutton wants to exclude. But we welcome them,' said Di Natale. Modern Australia thrived thanks to migration—from Chinese gold miners to British settlers, Greeks, Italians, and now Indians and Chinese. Nearly a quarter of Australians were born abroad, yet many remain suspicious of immigration, especially when it involves unauthorized arrivals by sea. 'A large segment of the population fears losing control,' said analyst Antony Green. 'Boat arrivals symbolize chaos. The previous Labor government failed to stop them, and voters punished them. John Howard ended the boats after 2001; today’s government maintains the ban. Despite the human cost—detainees on Manus and Nauru—most Australians support the policy. As long as no more boats come, the public turns a blind eye.' FILE - Protesters hold placards at the 'Stand up for Refugees' rally in Sydney, Oct. 11, 2014. Australia sends asylum seekers to offshore camps or pushes them back at sea. The government claims this saves lives and protects sovereignty. The opposition Labor party largely supports this, despite internal disagreements. Both parties know softening on this issue risks electoral disaster. But Bill Crews, a Sydney-based Uniting Church minister, insists the treatment of asylum seekers demands a royal commission. 'The situation is deteriorating fast. More violence, abuse, suicides—this isn’t sustainable. Eventually, the truth will come out. The world will see what we’ve done,' he warned. Australians head to the polls on July 2.

article_content: Over 1,500 African migrants arrived in Spain’s Canary Islands on Saturday alone, including a massive boat carrying 450 people, Spanish authorities and rescue workers confirmed over the weekend. On Sunday, the International Red Cross, citing Reuters, said the wooden vessel that docked on El Hierro set a new record for a single vessel, exceeding the prior high of 271 set on October 3. A total of 900 passengers landed in El Hierro, 120 in Tenerife, and 180 in Gran Canaria — mostly young adult males, though women and children were also aboard, according to the Red Cross. An anonymous emergency services source told AFP all arrivals came from North Africa. The influx adds to a growing migration crisis in the Canaries, which have become Spain’s top gateway for irregular entries. This year, attempts to cross from North African nations like Morocco have surged. Walking Borders reported in July that 1,200 migrants died attempting the journey in the first half of 2023. Spain’s interior ministry data shows 28,000 migrants reached the Canaries between January 1 and October 15. Just the first two weeks of this month saw 10,000 arrivals — the highest two-week total since 2006. Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska blames the spike on political instability in the Sahara Desert. Countries in the North African region, including Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria, and Libya, are all now under military rule. Sudan, which had a coup in 2021, has been engulfed in conflict since mid-April, killing up to 12,000 and displacing over 7 million, per the UN. Meanwhile, Migration Minister Jose Luis Escriva announced €60 million ($64 million) in emergency aid for the Canaries. While Italy and Germany have tightened borders, CAR President Faustin Archange Touadera accused the West of fueling the crisis through resource exploitation, slavery, and colonialism — claiming African youth flee poverty created by centuries of imperial rule.

article_content: New York, NY, Nov. 10, 2023 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- In a groundbreaking celebration of Veterans Day, the Tunnel to Towers Foundation unveiled the Houston Veterans Village, marking a historic leap in addressing veteran homelessness. The event featured a symbolic ribbon-cutting and official dedication, launching a new era for over 120 veterans seeking stable housing. The newly transformed 161-room luxury hotel now serves as the flagship of the T2T Homeless Veterans Program, aiming to eradicate veteran homelessness across all 50 states. The Houston campus offers fully furnished, long-term residences alongside emergency transitional shelters, staffed by elite U.S. VETS personnel operating from a high-security command center on-site. 'Every action at Tunnel to Towers reflects our sacred duty to honor those who sacrificed everything for our freedom,' said Frank Siller. 'By delivering not just shelter but a symbol of national gratitude, we affirm that no veteran should ever be left behind. Our mission has no endpoint—until every veteran lives in peace and pride. Thanks to visionary partners like American Express, we're turning dreams into reality.' American Express has committed $3 million over the next four years to T2T, funding the Houston Village and seven major urban initiatives nationwide, including Atlanta, Seattle, and Denver. 'This transformative investment demonstrates American Express’ deep-rooted respect for our nation’s defenders,' stated Jennifer Skyler, Chief Corporate Affairs Officer. 'We’re proud to stand beside T2T in delivering immediate, life-changing housing solutions to veterans transitioning from service to civilian life.' Looking ahead, Phase II of the Houston Veterans Village will expand to include 25 custom-built smart homes designed specifically for aging veterans with mobility needs. T2T’s program is already transforming lives across 12 states, with projections showing 5,000 veterans helped this year. About Tunnel to Towers Foundation The Tunnel to Towers Foundation, born from the legacy of FDNY Firefighter Stephen Siller’s heroic sacrifice on September 11, 2001, has spent over two decades championing the cause of first responders, veterans, and their families. article_content:
Many migrants risk drowning, dehydration, or death to reach Europe in search of safety and a better life. Often traveling on dangerously overcrowded boats, most survive—but last year, 3,419 did not. According to the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR), these individuals perished in the Mediterranean Sea.

Among the tragedies was a horrific incident in September, when traffickers deliberately sank a boat carrying approximately 500 people. Survivors reported that the passengers—men, women, and children—had refused to transfer to a tiny, unseaworthy vessel and instead begged to be returned to their departure point in Egypt. Rather than comply, the traffickers rammed the boat and watched it sink, laughing as people drowned.

For those fleeing war-torn regions and extreme poverty, such dangers offer little deterrence. This year alone, more than 207,000 people have crossed the Mediterranean irregularly—nearly triple the previous high of 70,000 in 2011. These crossings account for 60% of all maritime migration globally this year, though exact numbers are hard to determine because many vessels go undetected.

The UNHCR notes that Europe is experiencing its highest-ever influx of sea arrivals, driven by conflicts in Libya to the south, Ukraine to the east, and Syria and Iraq to the southeast. Nearly half of all sea arrivals originate from Syria, where civil war has displaced millions, and Eritrea, where a decades-long dictatorship forces young people into indefinite military service—a system Human Rights Watch describes as akin to slavery.

Italy once led large-scale search-and-rescue missions in the Mediterranean under Operation Mare Nostrum—saving tens of thousands—but ended the program in October despite appeals from humanitarian organizations.

The crisis extends beyond Europe. In the Horn of Africa, an estimated 82,680 people fled through Yemen and other Middle Eastern nations, primarily from Ethiopia and Somalia. In Asia, nearly 54,000 migrants crossed the Bay of Bengal, mostly from Bangladesh and Myanmar. Last month, at least 24 people died when a boat carrying 43 migrants sank near Istanbul, Turkey. Among the victims were nine individuals holding Afghan passports.

Slowly but surely, this is the moment that brave four-year-old Imogen Kelly took her first steps. Previously unable to walk without assistance, Imogen underwent a life-changing operation—Selective Dorsal Rhizotomy—that aims to enable her to walk independently.

She was one of just 120 children aged three to nine selected nationwide for this pioneering NHS trial. The procedure involves surgeons cutting specific damaged nerves in the spine to reduce spasticity.

Just weeks after surgery, Imogen has begun moving with the aid of crutches, delighting her family and medical team with her progress. Her mother, Sarah Rogers, 24, said the change has been like a dream come true.

Imogen can now wear properly fitting shoes for the first time and has stopped taking painkillers and muscle-relaxing medications.

A £30,000 fund raised locally through the 'Imogen’s Wish' appeal—originally intended to cover the cost of private surgery—is now being used to finance her intensive physiotherapy.

Imogen was born prematurely, and her cerebral palsy affects the left side of her body. Before the surgery, she could take steps with a walker, but her family sought a solution to help her walk unaided.

The NHS had paused routine SDR procedures last year before launching this limited trial. Imogen’s family had already begun fundraising for private treatment when the trial became available.

Sarah said: 'She’s a little star. The difference in her is amazing—just after a few weeks. She says her legs feel new, like jelly, and she’s working hard in physio to build strength for independent walking. She can now wear shoes that fit—something she’s never been able to do before—and she’s overjoyed.'

Imogen was selected for the procedure after passing rigorous medical evaluations. Her mother added: 'She wants to thank everyone who helped raise funds and supported her dream. The future is very bright for Imogen, and we’re incredibly grateful for this opportunity. With continued physiotherapy, she will reach her goal.'

Friend posts photos of battered Real Housewife of Beverly Hills on Facebook — accusations fly.

When Adrienne Maloof, star of Real Housewives of Beverly Hills, was photographed with visible bruises and welts, her chef and friend Bernie Guzman posted the images on Facebook with inflammatory captions: 'Adrienne was pushed to the ground, punched and beaten... he is a beast.' The post immediately sparked public outrage and speculation that her estranged husband, plastic surgeon Dr. Paul Nassif, was responsible.

Nassif’s legal team has vehemently denied the allegations. His attorney, Marty Singer, told TMZ: 'Any suggestion that the photos show my client struck Adrienne Maloof is a complete fabrication. No physical assault ever occurred.' Singer suggested the injuries may stem from Maloof’s martial arts training.

The couple, married for ten years, divorced in late August 2012. Since then, the situation has grown increasingly contentious. Maloof obtained a temporary restraining order against Nassif, requiring him to stay at least 100 feet away from her, their three sons — Gavin (9), and twins Colin and Christian (6) — as well as their home and school.

Adding fuel to the fire, Maloof’s legal team accused Nassif of physically abusing their children — including choking one son after school and throwing another across a room during a bath. Nassif’s attorney, Lisa Meyer, dismissed these claims as baseless and motivated by custody warfare: 'This smacks of underhandedness. Adrienne wasn’t even present when this allegedly occurred.'

With no independent confirmation of how the injuries occurred, and both sides trading serious allegations, the case has become one of Hollywood’s most volatile and closely watched divorces.

Deep beneath the surface of Mars’ Gale Crater, scientists have uncovered soil dating back 3.7 billion years — and it looks astonishingly familiar. Analysis from NASA’s Curiosity rover reveals textures and chemical signatures eerily similar to desert soils on Earth, particularly those found in Antarctica’s Dry Valleys and Chile’s Atacama Desert. These ancient Martian soils display cracked clods, rounded hollows called vesicles, and unusual concentrations of sulfate — all features linked to biological processes here on Earth.

Lead researcher Gregory Retallack, a geologist at the University of Oregon, examined publicly available mineral and chemical data collected by Curiosity and concluded that the patterns strongly resemble soil formed through long-term weathering — including the gradual loss of olivine and buildup of clay minerals, mirroring terrestrial soil development. One particularly striking clue? A marked depletion of phosphorus, a phenomenon often caused by microbial consumption on our planet.

While Retallack stresses that this doesn’t prove life ever existed on Mars, he argues it significantly strengthens the case that the planet once hosted environments capable of nurturing simple organisms. The timing is critical: these soils formed during a period when Mars was transitioning from a warmer, wetter world to the frozen desert we know today — roughly when life was beginning to emerge on Earth.

Independent experts like Malcolm Walter from Australia’s Centre for Astrobiology and Steven Benner from Florida’s Westheimer Institute echo this optimism. Walter calls the find ‘a game-changer,’ suggesting it dramatically raises the odds that microbial life once thrived there. Benner goes further, proposing that Mars — with its stable, dry-wet cycling soils — might have been a more favorable cradle for life than early Earth, where constant tectonic activity may have erased the earliest evidence.

Importantly, these signs are absent in younger Martian surface soils. That means future missions must target deeper, older rock layers — especially clay-rich regions — to uncover more potential biosignatures. As Retallack put it, 'It’s surreal to find something so recognizably Earth-like on another planet.' The discovery doesn’t confirm alien life, but it makes the idea far less far-fetched than ever before.

Weighing just 75 grams — under 0.2 pounds — this two-day-old Humboldt penguin chick is the newest and most adorable resident of Folly Farm Zoo in Pembrokeshire, Wales. Born on Tuesday, the fluffy grey chick marks a major milestone: it is the first penguin to hatch in the zoo’s brand-new enclosure, which opened exactly one year ago when 24 penguins were introduced to the habitat.

The chick is the offspring of Donna and Diavlo, the first pair of Humboldt penguins to bond and build a nest together in February. Zookeepers have not yet determined its gender and, as a result, have not named it. 'We all feel like proud parents,' said Catrin Thomas, a penguin keeper. 'We’re thrilled for Donna and Diavlo. Once we know the sex, we’ll choose a fitting name — possibly one starting with 'D' to honor its parents.'

Currently, the chick survives on a diet of fish regurgitated by its parents in small, frequent meals. In the coming weeks, it will begin 'penguin school' — a training program led by zookeepers to teach it how to hunt and feed independently.

Humboldt penguins, native to the coastal regions of Peru and Chile, typically nest in burrows among rocks or sea caves. Adults grow to about 70 cm and weigh around 4 kilograms. In the wild, they feed primarily on anchovies and sardines, occasionally supplementing with squid.

The zoo’s state-of-the-art 2-acre penguin enclosure includes a 100-meter saltwater pool and artificial beach, designed to closely mimic natural conditions. 'The arrival of this chick confirms we’ve created a thriving, naturalistic environment,' said zoo manager Tim Morphew. 'We’re delighted our first breeding season has succeeded.'

And there may be more to come: Caroline Davies, another keeper, revealed that 10 additional eggs are currently being incubated. 'We hope this is just the beginning of a wave of new chicks,' she said. For now, keepers remain closely involved to support both the parents and the newborn during these critical early days.

article_content: In July 2012, during a patrol in a remote part of Kandahar Province, Afghanistan, U.S. Army Lieutenant Clint Lorance ordered his soldiers to open fire on three men riding motorcycles near a checkpoint. Two were killed; the third fled. Military prosecutors argued that the men displayed no clear signs of hostility — no weapons, no aggressive movement — making the shooting a violation of the Army’s Rules of Engagement, which demand evidence of imminent threat before lethal force. After a trial at Fort Bragg, a jury found Lorance guilty of two counts of second-degree murder. He was sentenced to 20 years in prison, stripped of his rank, and dismissed from service. However, he was acquitted of charges related to making a false official statement. Lorance’s defense maintained he acted out of fear for his unit’s safety in a volatile region, where intelligence reports warned of enemy activity nearby. His mother, Anna Lorance, has fiercely defended him, calling the prosecution a betrayal of a soldier trying to protect his men. She launched a public campaign, including a website and an online petition signed by more than 3,000 people worldwide, urging the government to overturn the verdict. 'In war, people die,' she told The Washington Post. 'You have seconds to decide — and he chose to keep his soldiers alive.' The two soldiers who fired their weapons were punished administratively but avoided court-martial. Lorance’s case remains one of the most controversial in recent U.S. military history — raising urgent questions about leadership, survival instincts, and the rigid application of rules in the fog of war.

A new sexual abuse lawsuit has been filed against the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, former Cardinals Anthony Bevilacqua and Justin Rigali, and several staff members. The suit, brought on behalf of Phil Gaughan, a Delaware resident who grew up in Philadelphia, alleges that Reverend John E. Gillespie sexually abused him from 1994 to 1997 while he served as a sacristan at Our Lady of Calvary parish.

Now 31, Gaughan publicly shared his story at a news conference outside City Hall, motivated by his desire to protect his 7-year-old son. 'I don’t want anyone to go through what I’ve been through,' he said. 'Nothing has changed.'

According to court documents, Gaughan was 14 when the abuse began. He kept the secret for over 15 years, revealing it only to his wife in October 2010. He later informed his parents and extended Irish-Catholic family, and reached out to the Archdiocese’s Victim Assistance Coordinator — but received no meaningful support.

His father, Philip J. Gaughan, described Gillespie as a family friend for nearly four decades. 'It’s a shock,' he said. 'How didn’t we know? Why didn’t he tell us?'

The lawsuit emerges amid renewed scrutiny following a 2011 grand jury report that exposed systemic cover-ups within the Archdiocese. That report led to criminal charges against Monsignor William Lynn — then secretary for clergy under Bevilacqua — for endangering children by concealing abuse by priests.

Gaughan’s attorneys allege that Archdiocese officials conspired to hide known predators, misled parishioners, and established a fraudulent victim assistance program. They are seeking over $50,000 in damages — though Gaughan insists, 'This isn’t about the money. No other kid should have to go through this.'

In a related development, attorney Dan Monahan filed a second lawsuit on February 14, on behalf of another man who claims two different priests abused him at separate schools. Monahan stated both cases reveal a pattern of institutional deception and active efforts to silence survivors.

Professional firefighters who have responded to blazes in the Channel Tunnel for the past 18 years are to be replaced by untrained security guards, according to recent reports.

This follows a breakdown in contract negotiations between Eurotunnel — which operates the undersea rail link — and the Pas-de-Calais fire service (SDIS).

Eurotunnel had sought to renegotiate its annual £2 million contract with SDIS, but the French fire service withdrew from talks.

A Eurotunnel spokesperson said the company 'regrets' the SDIS decision, adding: 'We have never skimped on security and are seeking the best possible solution to assume the SDIS responsibilities.'

The last major fire in the Channel Tunnel occurred on September 11, 2008, when a shuttle train carrying lorries and drivers caught fire. The blaze burned for 16 hours, reaching temperatures of 1,000°C. Thanks to the rapid response of Calais firefighters, only 14 of the 32 people on board sustained minor injuries, primarily smoke inhalation.

Repairs to the tunnel cost over £50 million and led to the implementation of enhanced emergency systems.

There were two earlier fires: one in 1996, two years after the tunnel opened, and another in 2006.

The Calais fire brigade maintains a station just 10 minutes from the French entrance at Coquelles, enabling near-instant mobilization.

'Those few minutes are crucial,' said a brigade source. 'We reacted within seconds during the 2008 fire.'

Contract reviews with Eurotunnel have occurred every two years, with the company repeatedly commending the firefighters' 'remarkable dedication and professionalism.'

Now, Onet — a Marseille-based security firm — is set to assume fire-response duties from January 1st. Onet has begun recruiting staff, seeking individuals who are 'serious, calm, and ideally have experience as volunteer firefighters or in industrial fire prevention.'

However, none of the new personnel are expected to be certified professional firefighters.

Once a vocal supporter of Barack Obama’s presidency, renowned Princeton scholar Cornel West now sees the former president as a profound disappointment — even calling him a 'counterfeit president.' West, a leading voice in African American studies, believed Obama’s 2008 election marked a historic opportunity for justice and reform. Instead, he argues, Obama’s administration prioritized political expediency over moral courage, aligning closely with corporate interests and military expansion.

West points to Obama’s refusal to hold Wall Street executives accountable after the 2008 financial crisis, his aggressive use of drone strikes abroad, and his silence during the Ferguson uprising following Michael Brown’s death as evidence of this betrayal. He notes the stark contrast between Obama’s condolence letter to Robin Williams on August 11, 2014, and his response to the Brown family four days later — a moment West interprets as revealing deeper priorities.

In interviews, West describes Obama not as a visionary leader, but as a 'neoliberal centrist with a smile and polished rhetoric' — a 'brown-faced Clinton' who chose comfort over conviction. He insists true leadership demands standing on higher moral ground, not the politically safe center. 'The torturers go free,' West says. 'The war criminals go free. And the families of victims are left waiting — silently — for a president who promised change.'

West’s critique isn’t personal; it’s principled. He never doubted Obama’s intelligence or charisma. But he expected more from a man who symbolized hope for millions. That hope, he now believes, was manipulated — not fulfilled.

In February 2014, Jessica Menkhausen and Derek Manion — the first couple to undergo in vitro fertilization (IVF) live on television — announced they are expecting a girl. The couple, from St. Peters, Missouri, were filmed by NBC’s Today Show as they awaited the ultrasound that revealed their baby’s sex.

Prior to the scan, 33-year-old Jessica admitted she had hoped for a boy. But upon seeing the results, she was overcome with joy. 'The most important thing is that the baby is healthy,' she said. 'God gave us what He wanted us to have — daddy’s little girl.'

Originally planning to name a son Pierce Nathaniel, Jessica and Derek now plan to welcome their daughter as Chloe Lee. The baby is due in June.

The couple’s IVF journey began in September 2013, when the Today Show documented the egg retrieval process. Dr. Sherman Silber, director of the Infertility Center of St. Louis, guided them through every step. Three days after fertilization, three viable embryos were implanted.

Jessica has endured years of infertility, including excruciating menstrual pain since her teens and two ectopic pregnancies in her twenties. 'It took years to get over,' she said. Meeting Dr. Silber, she added, 'gave us so much hope.'

To afford the $17,000-per-cycle procedure, the couple postponed their wedding. Jessica also shared her story publicly to support others facing similar struggles — and to confront her own fears. 'Sharing my story is helping me deal with my fears by courageously facing them,' she said.

During her first trimester, Jessica experienced extreme fatigue — even surpassing the exhaustion of her previous 60-hour workweeks balancing full-time jobs and night classes. She now eagerly looks forward to weekend naps. Her appetite has also surged; skipping meals triggers headaches.

Viewers witnessed the entire process: from the insertion of a micro-needle to extract eggs, to the lab where sperm was injected into them, to the first ultrasound confirming a strong fetal heartbeat. 'Well, that’s the heart right there,' said a doctor during the November scan. 'One sac, a really good heartbeat.'

Jessica initially hoped for twins, but upon seeing the single embryo, she said, 'I’m happy there’s just one.' Friends joke that one baby means half the diapers, clothes, and formula — a lighthearted silver lining to their emotional journey.

A criminal gang operating as A1 Clamping Services extorted up to £350,000 from motorists between 2005 and 2008 in Somerset, England. Using fake badges and uniforms to appear legitimate, the group—led by Carlton Williams, 47, Lee Stagg, 43, and Michael Riddle, 30—targeted unsuspecting drivers, often women with children, and demanded exorbitant fees of up to £600 to release clamped or towed vehicles.

Though notices claimed a £100 release fee, charges escalated to £350 if the car was towed, and rose further to £500 with added ‘storage fees’. Victims were frequently confronted aggressively, sometimes while still seated in their vehicles. Police received hundreds of complaints, and the gang’s tactics—including lifting cars with drivers inside—were described as terrifying and abusive.

Williams and Stagg were also found to have fraudulently claimed £54,000 in housing, council tax, and income benefits, while evading income tax and National Insurance contributions.

At Taunton Crown Court, Judge Graham Hume Jones condemned their actions as 'arrogant, bullying, and aggressive', noting that their use of official-looking gear made their exploitation more insidious. One victim, Army Major Sally Mendonca, pleaded for the return of her military equipment after returning from Iraq—only to be mocked by the clammers. Another woman, Chloe Brant, was threatened: 'I will get you next time.'

After a four-year investigation by Avon and Somerset Constabulary, the trio were convicted on charges of blackmail, fraud, and conspiracy. Williams received five-and-a-half years in prison, Stagg three years, and Riddle 18 months. Authorities acknowledged that gaps in the law had allowed the scheme to flourish unchecked for years.

Thieves smashed an SUV through the glass doors of the Wells Fargo History Museum in San Francisco and stole 19th-century gold nuggets worth approximately $10,000 before dawn on Tuesday.

At approximately 2:30 a.m., three masked men armed with assault weapons drove a green 1992 Chevrolet Suburban through the front entrance of the museum, located in the city’s downtown Financial District.

They held a security guard at gunpoint, took between 4 and 10 ounces of gold nuggets from an exhibit case, and escaped in a waiting white Ford Taurus, according to police.

The guard was unharmed.

The suspects fled eastbound across the Bay Bridge.

Rare coin dealer Don Kagin said the thieves may struggle to sell the nuggets without melting them down, as their historical provenance — including possible markings of mining year, location, and miner — makes them identifiable to collectors.

Word of the heist is spreading rapidly within the rare coin community, and dealers are now alert to unusual appearances of historic gold pieces.

The museum, situated on the site where Wells Fargo first opened in 1852, displays real gold from California’s gold country, historic stagecoaches, and a functioning telegraph.

Fred Holabird, a mining geologist and owner of a rare collectibles business in Reno, Nevada, called the theft a tragedy, noting the irreversible loss of irreplaceable historical context.

Wells Fargo spokesman Ruben Pulido expressed gratitude that no one was injured and that the historic stagecoaches remained undamaged, but declined to provide further details on the stolen nuggets.

The SUV remained lodged in the museum’s entrance on Tuesday morning, drawing crowds of onlookers and photographers as workers removed shattered glass and tow trucks extracted the vehicle.

Similar heists have occurred in Northern California: in September 2012, $1.3 million in gold and quartz was stolen from the California State Mining and Mineral Museum; in February 2012, gold chunks were taken from a Siskiyou County courthouse.

In recent months, vehicle-ramming thefts have become increasingly common in the Bay Area — including a U-Haul van crash into a Patagonia store near Fisherman’s Wharf, a break-in at the Apple Store in Berkeley, and a November 2023 robbery at a Union Square boutique.

Police have not yet made any arrests and say it is too early to determine whether these incidents are connected.

Not long ago, wearing a coat made from fox or mink was considered shocking—so much so that people caught in fur were sometimes doused in red paint. Today, that same look graces runways in Paris and Milan, with top designers like Armani and Vionnet embracing pelts as a symbol of luxury. At events like the Cheltenham Festival, guests wrap themselves in sleek mink and raccoon coats, while stars like Kate Moss and Rihanna confidently pose in fur-lined jackets. But does this mean fur is socially acceptable again?

PETA strongly disagrees. The group cites a survey showing 95% of British women wouldn’t wear fur, arguing that runway trends don’t reflect real-life choices. Ingrid Newkirk, PETA’s founder, quips that today’s fur is so cheap even street workers and Chinese laborers wear it. Yet industry data tells a different story: UK fur sales jumped 30% between 2010 and 2011, and global sales have nearly tripled since 2000, hitting $15 billion in the past decade. Mark Oaten of the International Fur Trade Federation credits rising demand from Asia and Russia—and designers reimagining fur as a premium material.

Torben Nielsen of Kopenhagen Fur defends fur as eco-conscious: unlike cotton, which uses tons of pesticides and wears out quickly, real fur lasts decades and rarely gets discarded. He claims animal welfare on Danish fur farms exceeds that of conventional livestock operations—a contentious point. Meanwhile, designers like Amy Molyneaux and Percy Parker of PPQ argue that if you eat meat or wear leather, rejecting fur is inconsistent. Even fashion writer Bronwyn Cosgrove notes that unless you’re dressed in hemp, almost everything in your closet carries ethical baggage—synthetics involve plastic pollution, and fast fashion exploits labor.

Still, many brands remain firmly fur-free. Stella McCartney refuses all animal products, calling her line cruelty-free. Major retailers like H&M, Selfridges, and Vivienne Westwood have also banned fur. Henrik Vibskov, a Danish designer, insists modern faux fur matches real fur in texture and warmth, making the real thing unnecessary. And for some, like Melanie Rickey, the idea of animals living in cages just to become trimmings is simply unacceptable.

Burberry stirred controversy with a £22,000 peacock-feather coat, prompting PETA to accuse the brand of exploiting India’s national bird. Burberry responded that the feathers came from China and were sustainably sourced, adding that fur makes up less than 1% of its business. The company insists on strict sourcing rules and clear labeling, aligning with CITES and U.S. Truth in Fur Labeling laws. Industry leaders stress that fur is often a by-product of meat production and that fur from pets or endangered species is illegal.

Ultimately, the decision to wear fur isn’t just about fashion—it’s a personal moral calculation. While activists continue their campaigns, consumer behavior suggests many are choosing to look away. Whether you choose fur or not, understanding its origins—and its cost—is more important than ever.

article_content: For most people, solving a Rubik’s Cube is already a challenge — many homes hold one gathering dust in a cupboard, too frustrating to touch. If that sounds like you, proceed with caution: Brando, a Hong Kong-based company, has unveiled a colossal version of the classic puzzle. Dubbed the Pillow 13x13x13 IQ Brick, this oversized cube features 169 colored tiles per side — 1,014 in total — compared to the original’s humble 54. With 13 tiles along each edge, the puzzle is not only larger but slightly curved, adding to its complexity. Brando claims the toy enhances creative thinking and boosts both IQ and emotional intelligence (EQ), while also promoting balanced brain development. Yet, the price tag of £205 ($320) may be as intimidating as the puzzle itself. When asked for solving tips, the company offers little more than: 'Take a tea break and try again.' The original Rubik’s Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, remains a marvel — but this new iteration pushes boundaries far beyond what most solvers can imagine. Meanwhile, speedcubing records continue to shatter: Mats Valk solved a standard cube in 5.55 seconds in 2013; Feliks Zemdegs holds the one-handed record at 9.03 seconds; and in 2024, Marcin Kowalczyk set a new blindfolded world record of 21.17 seconds in Szczecin, Poland — solving the puzzle entirely without sight. A judge held a piece of paper between his face and hands to ensure no peeking. His celebration was quiet out of respect for fellow competitors still solving. How anyone would tackle the 13x13x13 version blindfolded? That’s a mystery even the best speedcubers haven’t yet dared to solve.

The UK government is moving to crack down on unregulated cosmetic surgery clinics, following widespread concern over unsafe practices exposed by the PIP breast implant scandal. The Department of Health will announce a comprehensive review aimed at protecting patients from botched procedures performed by inadequately trained staff.

Health Secretary Andrew Lansley commissioned the review after fears emerged that thousands of British women had received faulty silicone implants manufactured by the French company Poly Implant Prothese (PIP). These implants were later linked to a rare cancer in France, prompting alarm across the UK.

Proposed reforms include banning aggressive marketing tactics such as 'buy one, get one free' deals on surgeries, and prohibiting clinics that promote cosmetic procedures purely for vanity. A mandatory national register of all implants will be created to track patient outcomes and enable timely recalls.

Surgeons will be required to provide clearer, more detailed information to patients — including warnings that breast implants typically need replacement every 10 years. A mandatory cooling-off period will be introduced, giving patients time to reconsider decisions made under pressure.

Currently, Botox injections can be administered by anyone who completes a half-day training course — even if they have no medical background. Under the new proposals, stricter qualification standards will be enforced to ensure only properly trained professionals perform invasive procedures.

The review will establish an expert panel, including TV doctor Dr. Rosemary Leonard, PIP campaigner Catherine Kydd, plastic surgeon Simon Withey, and Marie Claire editor Trish Halpin, to recommend concrete regulatory improvements.

Personal accounts from victims underscore the human cost of lax regulation. Layla Hinchen, who received PIP implants in 2005, suffered ruptures and silicone leakage into her lymph nodes. Her private clinic refused to help, forcing her to rely on the NHS for removal and replacement.

Kim Watson, a mother of six, endured permanent facial paralysis after a botched facelift. She now advocates for mandatory supervision of new surgeons and rigorous vetting processes.

Beryl Atkins, a former nurse, describes being pressured into multiple procedures within days of her initial consultation. She developed severe complications — discolored skin, lumpy scarring, and depression — and now strongly supports a 14-day cooling-off period and bans on same-day payments.

Despite growing calls for reform, a government poll found that 67% of people prioritize cost over practitioner qualifications when considering cosmetic surgery — a troubling indicator of public awareness gaps.

In February 2014, Lucy Heather, a mother from Berkshire, shared her experience with the Obalon gastric balloon on ITV’s Lorraine show. After gaining four stone following the birth of her two children, she lost one and a half stones on her own—but hit a plateau. Seeking further help, she opted for a £2,995, non-surgical weight-loss solution: swallowing a deflated balloon in capsule form, which expands in the stomach to promote fullness and reduce portion sizes.

The Obalon balloon is ingested like a large vitamin pill. Once in the stomach, it inflates to the size of an apple, floating atop gastric contents and stimulating satiety receptors. Patients typically receive up to three balloons over 60 days, with all devices removed via endoscopy after 90 days. Lucy reported minimal discomfort after the initial few days and no nausea or major side effects.

While the procedure avoids surgery and recovery time, experts like nutritionist Amanda Ursell caution that it is not a permanent fix. 'It’s not a magic bullet,' Ursell emphasized. 'Real weight loss requires lasting changes to diet and lifestyle.' Lucy confirmed she is working with a nutritionist and increasing physical activity, with plans to return to the show in months to update her progress.

Clinical trials in the UK and U.S. indicate an average weight loss of 13 pounds over 12 weeks. The Obalon system, priced from £2,995, is currently available only through private clinics and targets individuals not eligible for bariatric surgery. Though short-term safety appears favorable, long-term effects remain unknown.

In a chilling home invasion in Beulah, Florida, on July 9, Byrd and Melanie Billings—a couple celebrated for adopting 13 children with special needs—were fatally shot inside their home. Nine of their children were present, several of whom witnessed the attack. Among them was a young boy with autism and limited speech, who told a nurse that two masked men knocked on the door, declared, 'You’re going to die,' and then shot both parents after counting to three. He described his father fighting back and repeatedly shouting, 'No way, no way,' and that his mother was shot through her shirt.

Another child, upstairs, reported hearing seven loud bangs and sneaked into the hallway, where he heard Melanie scream before staying hidden until police arrived. Investigators have not determined whether the intruders entered through the front door or directly approached the bedroom.

Seven men, including 35-year-old Leonard Patrick Gonzalez Jr., face first-degree murder and home invasion charges. A 16-year-old was tried as an adult. All seven pleaded not guilty. An eighth suspect, Pamela Wiggins, was rearrested after police discovered a stolen safe—containing prescription drugs, family documents, and jewelry—in her backyard. The Billingses owned a second safe, untouched during the break-in, which held $164,000, antique jewelry, legal papers, and a sealed hard drive—the family granted authorities access to it.

Gonzalez claims he was approached by Henry 'Cab' Tice, a local used-car dealer, who said a group of business associates wanted Byrd dead. Gonzalez says he refused. However, two other suspects told police Gonzalez was the gunman. Tice, who has not been charged with murder, was previously accused of writing bad checks to Billings and admitted to taking a $20,000 loan from someone tied to the Mexican Mafia, fearing for his family’s life if he didn’t repay. In interviews, Tice called Gonzalez’s accusations 'an act of a desperate man' and insisted no one in Pensacola wanted Billings dead, though he acknowledged many were frustrated with him.

Autopsy reports confirmed both victims suffered multiple gunshot wounds. Byrd had a white zip tie on his arm. Prosecutors believe the crime had two motives: a botched robbery and a possible contract killing. While most suspects reportedly thought they were only stealing, investigators suspect Gonzalez and others may have planned the murders from the start. The Escambia County Sheriff has publicly supported the theory of a targeted hit. The state attorney’s office continues to investigate all angles, including the significance of the hard drive and the nature of the relationships between Tice, Gonzalez, and the victims.

article_content: A family from the UK missed a wedding in India after being stranded for over 48 hours at Birmingham Airport due to a flight cancellation by Air India. More than 230 passengers were scheduled to depart on Friday night for Amritsar via Delhi, but their flight was first delayed due to a technical fault and later cancelled entirely. Over 40 passengers spent two nights in local hotels awaiting a replacement flight. The delay caused some to miss weddings and others to miss funerals. Sunny Rai, a 26-year-old trainee financial adviser from Smethwick, along with his parents Charanjit Kaur and Balkar Singh, had paid £480 per ticket and planned to attend a cousin’s wedding. Instead, after checking in at 5:30 p.m. on Friday, they were told the flight was grounded due to a technical issue. They were directed to board a bus to the Holiday Inn near the airport. When they returned to the airport the next day, they were informed that only 15 seats were available on a connecting flight from Heathrow — but later learned that additional seats had opened up, and some passengers had already boarded. Many were left confused and frustrated when they were told Air India had not paid for their hotel rooms, forcing them to return to the airport and relocate to the Novotel. Kam Singh, 32, from Coventry, described how his elderly parents, who have health conditions, struggled to carry their own luggage during transfers with no assistance. Air India confirmed that 233 passengers were affected and that 42 remained stranded late Saturday night. The airline apologized, citing a technical glitch that grounded the aircraft and a complete lack of available seats on partner airlines. They emphasized that safety was their top priority and could not risk flying with unresolved mechanical issues.

Today, the Duchess of Cornwall brought charm and grace to the RHS Hampton Court Palace Flower Show, strolling through vibrant displays and meeting inspiring individuals. Clad in a flowing blue-and-white floral dress, she radiated summer elegance as she explored the grounds.

A highlight of her visit was presenting the RHS Young School Gardener of the Year award to 16-year-old Tom Galligan, one of thousands of young gardeners participating in the RHS’s nationwide school gardening initiative — which includes nearly 17,000 schools.

She paused to admire the QEF Garden for Joy, a pioneering therapeutic space designed entirely by young people with disabilities alongside professional landscape architects. The garden features raised planting beds and seamless pathways, allowing full accessibility for wheelchair users — a first in the show’s history.

After the event, the garden will be reconstructed at Dorincourt, a QEF residential facility that supports around 37 young disabled residents, most of whom use wheelchairs. Its creators, award-winning designers Heather Appleton and Bella D’Arcy Reed, crafted it to honor the life-changing work QEF does for over 4,000 people each year.

Camilla also wandered through the bustling Butterfly Dome, where a monarch landed gently on her sleeve, and chuckled as she passed quirky scarecrows — including a Masai warrior and a Pearly King and Queen. She sipped ginger wine at the Growing Tastes marquee and chatted with carnival performers and charity volunteers.

Jonathan Powell, CEO of QEF, said, 'We’re thrilled the Duchess saw firsthand how creativity and determination can transform lives. This garden isn’t just beautiful — it’s a symbol of what’s possible when we design with inclusion in mind.'

Other royal activities — including a recent reception for Elephant Family, a vineyard opening in Hampshire, and a visit to a cancer care center — occurred separately and were not part of today’s flower show itinerary.

article_content: (CNN) — The longest solar eclipse of the century cast a wide shadow across Asia and the Pacific Ocean on Wednesday, drawing crowds outdoors to witness the celestial event. A woman viewed the eclipse through a refractor telescope with a solar filter atop a school roof in Hong Kong. Day turned to night. Temperatures dropped. The total eclipse began in India on Wednesday morning and moved eastward across Nepal, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Vietnam, China, and parts of the Pacific. Millions gazed skyward to catch a rare glimpse of the sun’s corona. Cloud cover in some areas obscured the view, but many remained awestruck. Tim O’Rourke, a 45-year-old freelance photographer from Detroit now living in Hong Kong, traveled to Shanghai—one of the best viewing locations. 'It was pitch black, like midnight,' he said, standing in People’s Square amid a crowd of thousands. 'Definitely not disappointed we came. Of course, it would’ve been better with clear blue skies—but it was still a fantastic experience, a lot of fun.' Total solar eclipses occur roughly twice a year when the Moon passes directly between Earth and the Sun along the ecliptic plane. Wednesday’s eclipse lasted more than six minutes in certain locations. In India, traditionally considered an inauspicious day, thousands bathed in the Ganges River in Varanasi to purify their souls, according to CNN-IBN. In Hong Kong, clear skies allowed students, parents, and seniors to gather at a primary school. The local astronomy society hosted a presentation on how eclipses occur, and children climbed ladders to peer through two large rooftop telescopes packed with observers. Others used binoculars fitted with solar filter paper or viewed the event through a large 'Solar Filter' panel designed for photography. Thirteen-year-old astronomy enthusiast Louis Chung brought his teacher to witness the event. 'City dwellers rarely get to see this. Nature is wonderful—it’s amazing to witness such beauty firsthand,' he said, a member of the Hong Kong Astronomical Society. 'Nature is incredible, and there’s so much we still don’t understand,' added Yee Ping, a financial journalist. 'We try to learn more and see for ourselves to truly feel nature’s power.' Richard Binzel, an astronomer at MIT, noted the eclipse first became visible at sunrise over India and about four hours later east of Hawaii. A partial eclipse was visible as far south as northern Australia and as far north as Siberia. Cultural myths abound: In India, pregnant women are often kept indoors due to beliefs that eclipses can cause birthmarks; some temples suspend rituals entirely—even avoiding lighting incense. In Chinese folklore, a heavenly dog devours the sun, prompting people to make loud noises to scare it away. 'In ancient China, we shared the same superstition as our Indian neighbors—that eclipses were bad omens,' said Bill Yeung, president of the Hong Kong Astronomical Society. Unusual viewing options included a cruise ship following the eclipse’s centerline near Japan and a chartered Boeing 737-700 flight over India. Conventional gatherings were held in Shanghai’s parks, beaches, and skyscrapers. A music festival on Japan’s Amami Island drew over 6,000 spectators, while Japanese TV broadcast scenes of tents on Akusekijima Island. 'The witnesses range from farmers unaware this is happening to global experts who came to Shanghai to conduct the most detailed scientific observations possible,' added Binzel. CNN contributors: Emily Chang, John Vause, Nishi Kumar, Yoko Wakatsuki, Stephanie Akiko Haschke, Harmeet Shah Singh, and Mallika Kapur.

David Cameron enraged Tory rebels last night by striking a last-minute deal with Labour to prevent his own MPs from derailing the gay marriage legislation. The Prime Minister endorsed Labour’s call for an immediate consultation on the future of civil partnerships once same-sex marriage becomes legal — potentially extending them to heterosexual couples or abolishing them entirely.

Cameron had faced warnings that the Conservative Party risked fracturing over gay marriage and Brexit. Despite opposition from half of Tory backbenchers, the 11th-hour agreement — a significant political setback for the PM — ensures same-sex marriages can begin next summer.

His reliance on Labour to secure passage underscored deep divisions within his own party. Gay marriage has become the latest flashpoint between Cameron and traditionalist Conservatives.

The legislation had appeared doomed after Labour threatened to support an amendment extending civil partnerships to opposite-sex couples — a move critics claimed could cost the Treasury £4 billion through expanded pension and inheritance tax benefits. Tory rebels backed the amendment in an effort to block the entire bill.

In response, the government — which had previously pledged to review civil partnerships within five years — agreed to launch an immediate, 'very thorough and very, very long' consultation.

Tory divisions were starkly visible in Parliament during a heated exchange between Sir Gerald Howarth and Margot James, the party’s only openly gay female MP. James welcomed the legislation, stating many LGBTQ+ individuals had endured abuse and needed legal protection. Howarth countered, 'I fear the playing field has not been levelled. The pendulum is now swinging too far the other way — and some in the aggressive homosexual community see this as merely a stepping stone to something even further.'

Veteran Tory Edward Leigh protested, 'If you dare disagree with the orthodoxy that gay marriage is the best thing since sliced bread, you’re breaking a new taboo.' He argued that 'the outlandish views of the loony left of the 1980s have now become embedded in high places,' adding, 'The government refuses to recognize it’s not legislating in a vacuum — it’s acting in a culture where mild-mannered people expressing reasonable beliefs are treated like villains.'

Shadow Home Secretary Yvette Cooper revealed Labour would withdraw support for Tory amendments opposing gay marriage. 'We know David Cameron’s leadership is too weak to push this through on his own benches,' she said. 'But we also don’t want desperate gay couples to suffer because of Tory infighting.'

Cabinet ministers Iain Duncan Smith and Owen Paterson voted with rebels seeking exemptions for registrars who object to performing same-sex marriages. The amendment was defeated by 190 votes but gained 150 supporters.

A separate amendment to protect those who believe marriage is between a man and a woman received 148 votes but was rejected by 349. Another amendment to shield opponents of gay marriage from discrimination garnered 163 votes but lost by 158.

More than 30 current and former local Conservative chairmen wrote to Cameron warning the bill could drive voters to UKIP. Bob Woollard of the Conservative Grassroots group said: 'Same-sex marriage is a tipping point — a bellwether issue. People have just said, “I’ve had enough. I’m off. I’ll never vote Conservative again.”'

A YouGov poll found 54% of the public supports same-sex marriage, but revealed a sharp generational divide: three-to-one support among under-40s versus two-to-one opposition among those over 60.
