Former U.S. government contractor and intelligence whistleblower Edward Snowden has firmly denied allegations that he collaborated with the Russian government to leak classified documents about the National Security Agency’s surveillance programs, calling the claims 'absurd.'

His response followed remarks by Rep. Mike Rogers, chair of the House Intelligence Committee, who suggested Snowden’s presence in Moscow was no accident—implying he was taken under the 'loving arms' of an FSB agent. Snowden countered: 'I clearly and unambiguously acted alone, with no assistance from anyone, much less a government. It won’t stick, because it’s clearly false—and the American people are smarter than politicians think they are.'

Rep. Rachel McCaul of the House Homeland Security Committee echoed skepticism, stating she believes Snowden was 'cultivated by a foreign power,' though she admitted she lacks definitive proof.

Snowden pointed to his 40-day detention at Moscow’s Sheremetyevo Airport after fleeing the U.S. as evidence he was not being sheltered by Russian intelligence: 'Spies get treated better than that.'

This is not the first time Snowden has faced espionage accusations. Last year, he was wrongly accused of working for China—a claim he dismissed by asking: 'If I were a Chinese spy, why wouldn’t I have flown straight to Beijing? I could be living in a palace petting a phoenix by now.' He criticized the media for amplifying unsubstantiated theories instead of holding power accountable.

Meanwhile, President Barack Obama announced reforms to U.S. surveillance practices in a January 17, 2014 speech at the Department of Justice. He pledged to end the NSA’s bulk collection of telephone metadata—the records of calls, not their content—and to establish a new system that preserves national security capabilities without the government storing the data indefinitely. However, he affirmed that broad surveillance operations would continue as a counterterrorism measure.

According to Snowden’s Russian lawyer, Anatoly Kucherena, the whistleblower now fears for his life. Kucherena cited anonymous threats published by BuzzFeed, including one from a purported Pentagon official saying, 'I would love to put a bullet in his head,' and another from an NSA analyst declaring, 'In a world where I would not be restricted from killing an American, I personally would go and kill him myself.'

Kucherena emphasized that these statements represent real dangers and demanded accountability: 'We have specific publications that printed these interviews. We will ask for these people’s masks to come off. We must know who this NSA officer is.'

Snowden has lived under guard in Moscow since receiving temporary asylum in August 2013—a move that angered Washington and led President Obama to skip a summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Putin has repeatedly denied any collaboration between Russian intelligence and Snowden.

A woman has spoken of the horror she felt upon discovering that her late husband was, in fact, her biological father. Valerie Spruill, 60, of Doylestown, Ohio, made the shocking discovery through a DNA test after her husband, Percy, passed away.

Spruill, a mother of three and grandmother of eight, is sharing her story in hopes of locating siblings she never knew existed. 'It needs to be told, because children need to know where they come from,' she told the Akron Beacon Journal. 'And I know it hurts — because I have been devastated by this.'

The confusion began when she was placed in the care of her grandparents at three months old. Her mother, Christine, worked as a 'night lady' — a term she used — and testified in the 1980 trial of Summit County Probate Judge James Barbuto, who was later convicted of sexual offenses.

Valerie’s mother and father began a relationship when he was just 15. The exact number of their children remains unclear, but Valerie knows of six brothers. She was raised believing Christine was merely a family friend.

At age nine, she was heartbroken to learn Christine was her biological mother — meaning the man she thought was her father was actually her grandfather. But she was never told who her real father was.

Years later, she met and married Percy, a truck driver and parking lot attendant from Mississippi. He died in 1998 at age 60 after a brief illness. For years, Valerie had heard unsettling rumors about their relationship.

After Percy’s death, an uncle revealed the truth. She confirmed it with a DNA test, using hairs found on a brush in their home. She does not know for certain whether Percy was aware he had married his daughter, but she strongly believes he knew — and was too afraid to tell her.

Since his death, Valerie — now retired — has been seeing a therapist to cope with the trauma. She has also endured serious health issues, including a prolonged hospitalization, which she attributes to the emotional toll of uncovering this secret.

'My biggest goal is to find them and let them know that [their mother] loved them, no matter what,' she said. 'And to say, thank God she gave you away, like she gave me away — so you could have a beautiful life.'

article_content: A dramatic dashboard video captures the moment a TransAsia Airways ATR-72 plane lost control, clipped a bridge overpass, and crashed into the Keelung River in Taiwan. The aircraft, carrying 58 people en route from Taipei to Kinmen, went off course shortly after 11 a.m. local time. Thirteen people have been confirmed dead, 28 injured, and 17 remain missing. Rescuers worked tirelessly to recover survivors from the submerged wreckage, with some passengers seen wearing life jackets as they awaited rescue boats. The plane’s wing struck the Nanhu Bridge, also hitting a passing taxi — two occupants of the vehicle were injured but stabilized. Taiwan’s Civil Aeronautics Administration confirmed the aircraft was less than a year old and had undergone a safety inspection just weeks prior, on January 26. TransAsia Airways CEO Chen Xinde offered a heartfelt apology, noting that 31 of those aboard were Chinese tourists — including three children — from two travel agencies based in Xiamen. Twenty-two passengers were from Taiwan. Emergency personnel, including 165 military staff, were deployed to support rescue efforts. The Straits Exchange Foundation has coordinated with Beijing authorities, and teams have been sent to both the crash site and hospitals. This tragic event echoes a deadly 2014 crash involving another TransAsia ATR-72 near the Penghu Islands, which claimed 49 lives.

In a unique study funded with nearly half a million pounds from the UK’s Economic and Social Research Council, scientists from the Universities of Portsmouth, Exeter, and Royal Holloway are exploring how children form ideas about war and the military through play. Specifically, they’re examining popular dolls like HMAF — officially licensed by the UK Ministry of Defence — and classic action figures such as Action Man and GI Joe.

These dolls, dressed in realistic military gear including helmets, body armor, and even assault rifles, reflect imagery commonly seen in news coverage of conflicts like Afghanistan. Researchers aren’t trying to decide if such toys are ‘good’ or ‘bad.’ Instead, they want to understand how these everyday objects quietly shape British children’s views on security, service, and conflict — especially as media and real-world events blur together post-9/11.

Lead researcher Dr Tara Woodyer points out that play is often dismissed as trivial, yet it’s precisely this invisibility that makes it so influential. Toys don’t just mirror culture — they help build it. And while Barbie has long drawn scholarly attention, male action figures have been largely overlooked, despite their deep ties to national identity and militarized narratives.

Action Man, originally a British rebrand of the American GI Joe introduced in 1966, stopped being produced in 2006, but its legacy lives on in today’s military-themed dolls. The study, set to conclude in 2016, comes as British troops withdraw from Afghanistan — adding timely weight to its findings.

article_content: Queensland Premier Campbell Newman has stated that Russian President Vladimir Putin will not be welcome at this year’s G20 summit in Brisbane unless Russia fully cooperates with the international investigation into the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17. Seven residents of Queensland were among the 298 people killed when the passenger jet was struck by a missile over eastern Ukraine in July 2014. While Western officials suspect Russian-backed separatists used advanced weaponry supplied from Russia, Putin has consistently shifted blame to Ukraine. In a firm statement, Newman urged Putin to show good faith by supporting an impartial probe, saying, 'If he’s not willing to help uncover the truth, then Queenslanders don’t want him here.' Though the final decision on Putin’s invitation rests with Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott, Newman emphasized he was voicing the sentiment of many Queenslanders. Opposition Leader Bill Shorten echoed this call, labeling Russia’s alleged arms supply to Ukrainian rebels as 'reckless and stupid' and urging Abbott to reconsider inviting Putin if Moscow continues to obstruct the investigation. The UN Security Council has demanded a full, transparent inquiry, and protests against Putin’s potential visit are being held in Sydney. Flags across Queensland will fly at half-mast on Saturday to honor the victims.

Apple unveiled the iPhone 5 on September 12, 2012, introducing a new proprietary Lightning connector that replaces the 30-pin dock port used for nearly a decade across iPods, iPhones, and iPads.

This change renders thousands of existing Apple accessories incompatible unless users purchase an adapter. According to Gizmodo, the basic 'Lightning to 30-pin' adapter costs £18 (approximately $39), while a 0.2-meter cable version is priced at £24.

At the product launch, Phil Schiller, Apple’s Senior Vice President of Worldwide Marketing, explained the shift as inevitable progress: 'The iPhone from its start used the 30-pin connector, and it has served us well. A lot has changed — and it is time for the connector to evolve.'

The new Lightning port is slimmer, supports faster data transfer, and is reversible — allowing users to plug it in either direction. However, many consumers expressed frustration over having to repurchase accessories or adapters, viewing the move as a profit-driven strategy disguised as innovation.

On Sunday night, President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama celebrated their second inauguration with supporters at Washington D.C.’s National Building Museum, sharing heartfelt thanks and a rare glimpse into their personal lives. Michelle dazzled in a shimmering black cocktail dress and bold jewelry, while Obama proudly complimented her newly styled bangs — ‘She looks good. She always looks good,’ he joked. The evening was less about winning an election and more about honoring the nation they serve. 'We’re not here to celebrate a victory,' Obama told the crowd, 'we’re here to celebrate each other — and the incredible country we call home.'

The next morning, in a quiet White House ceremony, Obama took the oath of office again — this time using Michelle’s family Bible, surrounded by his wife and daughters Sasha and Malia. Chief Justice John Roberts administered the oath flawlessly, a contrast to the 2009 misstep. Later, in front of hundreds of thousands lining the Capitol steps, Obama delivered his inaugural address, calling on Americans to rise above division and tackle shared challenges: rebuilding the economy, confronting terrorism, reducing the deficit, and passing common-sense reforms on immigration and guns.

The day unfolded with tradition: a prayer by civil rights icon Myrlie Evers-Williams, stirring renditions of ‘America the Beautiful’ and the national anthem by James Taylor and Beyoncé, a poem by Richard Blanco, and a parade featuring 60 community groups. Though crowds were smaller than in 2009 — estimated between half a million and 700,000 — the spirit remained strong. Tourists and locals alike expressed pride, with one retiree from Texas noting, 'He’s more disrespected than any other president — but he’s trying for all of us.'

Even political rivals offered quiet support. Senator John Barrasso of Wyoming told CNN, 'We want any president to succeed — because when the president succeeds, America succeeds.' As the sun set, two inaugural balls closed the day, under skies dusted with snow. For Obama, the message was clear: leadership isn’t about applause — it’s about showing up, day after day, for something bigger than yourself.

Nestled high in the barren expanse of Chile’s Atacama Desert, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array—known as ALMA—is now operational as the most powerful and elevated radio telescope on Earth. Perched at nearly 5,000 meters above sea level, it’s roughly twice the height of Mount Fuji and halfway up the cruising altitude of a commercial airliner. Scientists here don’t just stare at the stars—they fight for every breath. Oxygen tanks are standard equipment, and most work is done remotely from a lower-altitude control center to avoid altitude sickness.

Rather than a single dish, ALMA is made up of 66 massive, movable antennas spread across the plateau, acting like one colossal eye. Together, they collect faint radio signals from the cosmos and combine them using a supercomputer, producing images ten times sharper than Hubble’s. This allows astronomers to peer through thick dust clouds and witness the birth of stars, planets, and even the molecular precursors to life—like water and organic compounds—that may have seeded Earth billions of years ago.

The location was selected not just for its height, but for its bone-dry air. Moisture absorbs the very signals ALMA is designed to detect, so this desert—one of the few places on Earth untouched by artificial light pollution—is ideal. The project, costing around £1 billion and involving partners from Europe, North America, and Asia, was built with one bold question in mind: Where did we come from?

British companies helped construct parts of the array, and the UK contributed £65 million to the effort. Though still ramping up to full capacity, ALMA has already begun delivering unprecedented views of distant galaxies and stellar nurseries. As one ESO spokesperson put it, it doesn’t just serve researchers—it reignites the childhood wonder of anyone who’s ever looked up at the night sky and asked, 'What’s out there?'

More than two years after the city of Christchurch was devastated by earthquakes, it has finally risen from the rubble — albeit in an unusual way. The city has built the world’s first cardboard cathedral, replacing the original 132-year-old Gothic cathedral destroyed in the February 2011 earthquake.

Much of Christchurch’s iconic architecture was flattened by the 6.3-magnitude quake, leaving New Zealand’s second-largest city deeply scarred.

The temporary Anglican cathedral opened last week, marked by a 10-day music series called 'Joyfully Un-munted,' according to RadioNZ.

The £2 million project features a 700-seat cathedral constructed from 98 interlocking cardboard tubes, each weighing 120kg. Designed by internationally renowned Japanese architect Shigeru Ban, the structure also incorporates timber, steel, and a concrete foundation.

The design was delivered by Christchurch-based firm Warren and Mahoney. Its colorful stained-glass windows add vibrancy to the otherwise industrial material.

Ban is known for pioneering emergency architecture using paper and cardboard. He previously built paper shelters in Haiti after the 2010 earthquake and cardboard homes following Hurricane Katrina in 2005.

The 2011 earthquake killed 185 people and injured many more, leaving Christchurch in ruins. Yet residents have responded with remarkable creativity.

Other initiatives, dubbed 'Gap Fillers,' have emerged across the city to temporarily replace lost infrastructure. For example, the site of the demolished Crowne Plaza Hotel now hosts a large pavilion made from over 3,000 wooden pallets. Opened in December, it provides much-needed space for small and medium-sized events.

Though temporary, the cathedral is engineered to last up to 50 years — a symbol of resilience and innovation in the face of tragedy.

A stash of raw tobacco worth £5 million in unpaid VAT and duty has been uncovered at an illegal cigarette factory in Bury, Greater Manchester.

Investigators from HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) raided an industrial unit and found three tonnes of dry, harvested tobacco leaves—enough to produce approximately three million cigarettes—alongside chemical drums, weighing scales, and fake packaging.

The tobacco, believed to have been imported from tobacco-growing countries, was being processed with glycerine, white spirits, vinegar, and vanilla to mimic hand-rolling tobacco.

Also discovered were £15,000 in cash and boxes of counterfeit branded packaging designed to deceive consumers into believing the product was legitimate.

The operation is part of 'Operation Eel,' a coordinated effort that included searches of two homes and a garage in the area.

Four men—two 35-year-olds from Bury and two from Blackburn aged 41 and 29—were arrested on suspicion of evading customs duties under the Customs and Excise Management Act. They have since been released on bail.

Investigations are ongoing, and the Bury site is being linked to other seizures in Essex, Preston, and Blackburn, which together have netted 11 tonnes of raw tobacco.

HMRC warns that counterfeit tobacco products contain unregulated and potentially harmful chemicals, with no quality control, and that purchasing them directly funds international organized crime.

Sandra Smith, Assistant Director of Criminal Investigation at HMRC, stated: 'Illicit tobacco factories hidden in our communities are packaging low-quality tobacco. Cheap tobacco may seem like a bargain, but there are no controls over what is mixed into the product—and by buying it, smokers are funding organized crime gangs.'

Doctors Without Borders (MSF) warned on Friday that thousands of children who fled the conflict in Sudan and sought refuge in neighboring Chad are now suffering from severe malnutrition. The humanitarian group urgently called for emergency food aid.

Chad hosts the highest number of Sudanese refugees, with over 900,000 already residing there. The situation has worsened in recent weeks as fighting intensifies in Sudan’s Darfur region. In the first week of November alone, more than 8,000 people crossed into Chad, according to the United Nations refugee agency.

At the Metche refugee camp, home to 40,000 people, MSF reported that 13.6% of children under five suffer from global acute malnutrition. Since the beginning of the year, MSF teams have treated approximately 14,000 malnourished children—nearly 3,000 of whom required hospitalization due to critical conditions.

According to estimates from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project, more than 10,400 people have been killed in the Sudan conflict. The UN reports that over 4.8 million have been internally displaced within Sudan, and another 1.2 million have fled to neighboring countries.

For over two decades, a dilapidated house at 19 Boonara Avenue in Bondi, one of Sydney’s most sought-after suburbs, has been an eyesore — its front yard and porch buried under towering piles of rubbish. The property, estimated to be worth between $1.8 million and $2.5 million, is now being auctioned by real estate agent Ric Serrao of Raine & Horne Double Bay.

The home, owned by sisters Mary, Elena, and Liana Bobolas, has long drawn criticism from neighbors and Waverley Council, who have repeatedly tried — and failed — to compel cleanup. More than $350,000 of public funds have been spent on waste removal since the issue first gained attention.

Despite the clutter — which includes broken appliances, cardboard boxes, glass bottles, rusted metal, and plastic bags — the property sits on a 550-square-meter block within walking distance of Bondi Beach. The listing describes the land as offering ‘plenty of scope to build your dream home’ (subject to council approval).

Neighbors report that the house has not been lived in for years, with no confirmed access to running water or electricity, yet the owners continue to guard the debris. A ginger cat has taken refuge among the ruins. Trees grow through the roof, and walls are riddled with holes.

In 2014, the council conducted a major cleanup, but many residents say conditions quickly reverted. One neighbor described the scene as ‘sickening’ and ‘filthy.’ Others have noted the Bobolas family appears primarily at night, occasionally seen sorting through the waste.

In the past six months, demand for young female apprentices in India’s manufacturing sector has surged four to fivefold, according to data from TeamLease Degree Apprenticeship. Driven by acute skilled labor shortages and a push to correct gender imbalances, companies are actively recruiting women who have completed Class 10 or 12 for on-the-job training roles.

Sumit Kumar, Chief Business Officer at TeamLease, noted that factories are becoming increasingly gender-neutral due to widespread talent gaps—India faces an estimated shortfall of 130 to 150 million skilled workers across industries. The rise is largely fueled by expansion in automotive, electric vehicles, electronics, and phone manufacturing.

Major employers such as Maruti Suzuki, MG Motors, Lumax, and ReNew are leading this shift. Women apprentices receive structured, three-year training in partnership with educational institutions, earning an initial monthly stipend of ₹13,000–15,000, which can increase with performance.

Executives highlight the value women bring to traditionally male-dominated shop floors. Rajesh Uppal of Maruti Suzuki said women introduce greater dynamism through diverse perspectives. The automaker is developing a strategy to significantly expand its female apprentice intake.

Maruti Suzuki trains over 3,000 apprentices annually from Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) and has partnered with the government to upskill 2,300 students yearly. Women are placed across departments including vehicle inspection and parts assembly.

MG Motors, in collaboration with Gujarat-based skill university Kaushalya, aims to upskill 100,000 students and target 50% gender diversity in its workforce, according to Sr. Director HR Yeshwinder Patial. Lumax, a top auto component maker, is targeting 30–35% female representation on its shop floors within the next 2–3 years, as stated by MD Dipak Jain.

At ReNew, women already make up 34% of its apprentice cohort. Co-founder Vaishali Nigam Sinha emphasized a 'grow our own timber' philosophy to build female talent within the renewable energy value chain, where women have historically been underrepresented.

Chinese actress Zhou Xun is a household name in China, yet remains relatively unknown beyond its borders. At 33, she has appeared on the covers of China’s editions of Harper’s Bazaar and Elle, but her presence in international markets has yet to take off. Zhou is humble about global recognition, expressing no desire to compete with Zhang Ziyi as the face of Chinese cinema abroad—instead, she simply aims to become a better actress.

Her latest role is in the historical epic 'Confucius,' co-starring Chow Yun Fat. But her breakthrough came in 2000 with 'Suzhou River,' after which Chinese media crowned her one of the country’s four top young actresses alongside Zhao Wei, Xu Jinglei, and Zhang Ziyi. Since then, she has carved a unique path through unconventional roles: a shy lab technician in 'All About Women,' a chain-smoking, alcohol-fueled spy in 'The Message,' and more.

Her performances have earned her accolades including Best Actress at the 2000 Paris Film Festival for 'Suzhou River', plus multiple Chinese film awards for 'Perhaps Love' (2005) and 'The Equation of Love and Death.' Born into a middle-class family, Zhou was training at a dance academy when a film director noticed her and urged her to pursue acting.

'Being an actress in China, I’m incredibly fortunate,' she told CNN. 'Especially now, as Chinese films grow more diverse and reach audiences overseas.' She believes the essence of acting transcends borders: 'It’s about understanding life, approaching every role with integrity. Ultimately, it comes down to being a good person—and acting responsibly.'

Though she champions responsibility, she doesn’t shy from method acting extremes—for 'The Message,' she arrived on set intoxicated to authentically portray an alcoholic spy. Despite endorsing luxury brands, Zhou remains refreshingly candid about her imperfections. 'Everyone has many faces,' she says. 'I have my bad sides too. We’re all trying to improve. I have plenty of shortcomings—it’s probably 50-50.'

In August 2013, Scott Phillips, former athletic director at East Memorial Christian Academy in Prattville, Alabama, resigned after refusing to become a member of the school’s affiliated church, East Memorial Baptist Church. Although he was never a member prior to his hiring in June 2012, Phillips was informed that church membership was a requirement for the athletic director role — a policy reportedly unwritten and unmentioned in his contract.

A devoted educator and coach, Phillips had previously taught Bible and science and served as boys’ basketball and assistant football coach. To meet expectations, he spent a year shuttling his family between the school’s 9 a.m. Baptist service and the 11 a.m. service at Church of the Highlands in Montgomery — his long-time congregation.

By summer 2013, exhausted by the dual attendance, Phillips approached school administrators requesting permission to return to his original church. He did not ask to leave his coaching duties — only to be excused from mandatory church membership. He offered to accept a demotion if necessary, but the administration refused.

After two meetings in late June, Phillips was asked to resign. The school later stated that ‘it was made very clear’ during hiring that the AD must be a faithful member of East Memorial Baptist Church. Phillips, however, insists the requirement was never disclosed in writing or verbally before accepting the position.

'If it had been in my contract, I possibly would not have taken the job,' Phillips told the Montgomery Advertiser. 'I was totally committed to East Memorial. I thought I proved I could do my job well without being a member.'

The school maintains that Phillips resigned after months of prayerful discussion. Yet Phillips remains puzzled: 'I was an advocate of East Memorial as athletic director. That’s what I thought my role was.'

By Martha De Lacey. PUBLISHED: 04:46 EST, 17 January 2013. | UPDATED: 11:20 EST, 17 January 2013.

A woman who once spent £80 per week — over £4,000 annually — on takeaways and weighed more than 17 stone has transformed her life, ditching fast food and losing more than a third of her body weight.

Sarah Jackson, from Coventry in the West Midlands, was once a size 24 and consumed large portions of greasy takeaways four times a week, costing nearly £400 monthly. But after breaking down in a changing room when she couldn’t fit into a pair of size 18 jeans, the 34-year-old mother of two resolved to change.

She has since lost over six stone and now wears a size 10. Sarah recalls her former diet: 'I would have sweet and sour chicken, rice, and chips from the Chinese almost every night. My portions were big enough for four or five people.'

The weight gain had affected her health: it took her 15 minutes to get out of bed, and she exercised zero. She avoided mirrors, clothes shopping, and social events due to shame and depression.

Sarah and Mark, a construction project manager, have been together 14 years and have two daughters. They never married because Sarah felt too embarrassed to wear a size 18 wedding dress.

Her daily meals included five chocolate digestive biscuits and an Innocent smoothie for breakfast; two sausage rolls, two pizza bread sticks, a chicken baguette from Greggs, and a can of Coca-Cola for lunch; and for dinner, Chinese takeaways (sweet and sour chicken, egg fried rice, chips, prawn crackers, and rose wine), Indian meals (chicken tikka masala, fried rice, chips, garlic naan), large pepperoni pizzas, kebabs (doner or chicken with chips), or home-cooked dishes like chicken chasseur with mashed potatoes and full-fat butter.

After joining Weight Watchers, she lost 6.5 pounds in her first week. Today, she leads her own class and teaches others how to manage their weight.

She still allows herself one takeaway per week — typically half a portion of chicken chow mein with extra bean sprouts, no rice or chips.

Sarah now walks and jogs regularly and runs three times a week. In just over a year, she lost 6st 1.5lbs and says, 'I’m a completely different person.'

She created an inspirational YouTube video titled 'The Power of a Weight Watchers Meeting' and hopes to lose another stone by summer.

Pratik Gupta, CEO & Co-Head of Kotak Institutional Equities, says: 'While we remain highly positive on the long-term and medium-term outlook for the Indian economy, investors must anchor their portfolios to valuations — what is already priced in — and the risk of disappointment. Geopolitical risks remain significant.'

'Large caps appear far more attractive to us than small and midcaps,' he added. For context, the Nifty is up about 7% year-to-date, while small- and mid-cap indices have risen 28–30%. Many individual stocks in these segments have performed even better.

Gupta notes that many small- and mid-cap stocks are trading well above their pre-Covid valuations — a trend not普遍 seen among large caps. Despite the recent rally, valuations remain the primary driver of his team’s allocation decisions.

Within large caps, private banks are favored due to attractive valuations and a multi-year banking upcycle. Loan growth is expected to remain robust, with Net Interest Margins stable and credit costs low. Deposit franchises are strengthening, making private banks — especially those with strong liability bases — appealing.

PSU banks also offer similar appeal — solid fundamentals, low credit risk, and reasonable valuations. The insurance sector — particularly life insurers — is another area of interest, along with real estate. Gupta highlights that real estate companies have significantly reduced leverage, pre-sales are rebounding, and cash flows are improving. Domestic interest rates may have peaked, further supporting the sector.

Consumer staples are gaining favor as rural demand recovers post-monsoon, raw material prices decline, and pre-election spending increases. While inflation has pressured margins recently, Gupta believes the worst is behind them. Consumer staples are preferred over discretionary goods, where demand remains weak and valuations less compelling.

Regarding capex, Gupta distinguishes between central government, state government, PSU, private, and MNC-driven investment. He cautions that central government capex growth is unlikely to continue at recent paces due to fiscal consolidation targets — the fiscal deficit must fall from 5.9% in FY24 to 4.5% by FY26. State governments face similar pressures.

Private capex shows encouraging signs, but growth is slower than market expectations. Companies with strong balance sheets and cost discipline will benefit most. Investors should avoid overpaying for capex-themed stocks based on optimistic assumptions.

In summary, Gupta recommends focusing on private banks, PSU banks, insurance, real estate, and consumer staples — sectors offering better risk-reward profiles amid elevated valuations elsewhere.

New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg has launched a new public health initiative aimed at reducing youth smoking by requiring retailers to conceal tobacco products behind counters, in cabinets, or under curtains — visible only during purchases or restocking. The move follows the recent court rejection of his 16-ounce sugary drink ban, another controversial effort to combat obesity.

Bloomberg argues that making cigarettes less visible will discourage young people from seeing smoking as normal. 'Smoking is going to kill these kids,' he told CNN’s Jake Tapper, warning that tobacco use undermines future career and educational opportunities.

Critics, including the New York Association of Convenience Stores and Altria Group (parent company of Philip Morris), call the plan excessive and unsupported by evidence. 'The notion of forcing law-abiding retailers to hide their inventory is patently absurd,' said NYACS President Jim Calvin, challenging the assumption that mere visibility drives youth smoking.

Supporters, including Health Commissioner Dr. Thomas A. Farley, point to declining adult smoking rates and stable teen smoking rates since 2007 as reasons to act. Farley calls the proposal a necessary next step in protecting adolescents.

A companion bill, the Sensible Tobacco Enforcement bill, aims to crack down on illegal cigarette sales and tax evasion by increasing penalties for unlicensed sellers and banning discounted tobacco products — while still allowing advertising and price displays.

New York has a long history of aggressive anti-smoking laws, beginning with the 1988 Smoke Free Air Act and expanding through 2011 to include parks and beaches. If passed, this tobacco display ban would make New York the first U.S. city to implement such a rule.

Two Dutchmen, Henri Van Doesburg, 68, and Arnold Van Milt, 49, have been sentenced to a combined 36 years in prison after being convicted of orchestrating a sophisticated, James Bond-style plot to smuggle £16.2 million worth of cocaine into the United Kingdom.

The drugs — 240 pounds (108 kilograms) of high-purity cocaine — were concealed within a hidden hatch in the rudder compartment of the Colombian vessel Cape Maria, moored off the coast of Scotland.

Van Doesburg and Van Milt planned to retrieve the shipment using Seabob underwater scooters, wetsuits, and a high-powered ribbed boat, operating under the cover of darkness to avoid detection.

Police uncovered the scheme after seizing the cocaine during a routine inspection of the Cape Maria in May. Van Milt was arrested near the ship in Seamill, where authorities also found his car equipped with the full set of underwater retrieval gear.

Van Doesburg was apprehended the following day in Aalsmeer, the Netherlands, after police traced encrypted communications from a Blackberry device linked to Van Milt. Forensic examination of his laptop revealed detailed records of the Cape Maria’s movements, as well as connections to two other vessels — the Indian Friendship and the Florentina — both of which had previously been intercepted carrying cocaine.

Van Doesburg’s son, Roderick, 23, and grandson, Darryl-Jay, 22, were arrested alongside the pair but were later acquitted after a four-week trial.

Prosecutors described the operation as a highly organized, months-long criminal enterprise, with the duo acting as a specialist 'drug retrieval service' for international trafficking networks.

Judge James Spencer QC, sentencing the pair at Leeds Crown Court, remarked: 'Despite your mature years, you played for high stakes — and you lost.'

The National Crime Agency and Border Force hailed the operation as a major disruption to organized crime, emphasizing that the seizure prevented millions of pounds’ worth of drugs from reaching UK streets.

article_content: During the fourth week of Casey Anthony’s murder trial, forensic experts clashed over whether duct tape found on Caylee Anthony’s skull was applied before or after her death. Dr. Werner Spitz, a defense pathologist, testified that the tape likely secured the jawbone after decomposition had removed soft tissue — not as a tool of suffocation. This contradicts the prosecution’s claim that chloroform and duct tape were used to kill the 2-year-old. Spitz also criticized the original autopsy conducted by Dr. Jan Garavaglia, arguing that examining the interior of the skull is standard procedure, even in advanced decomposition cases. However, when pressed, he admitted no published protocol mandates such an examination, relying instead on decades of experience. Meanwhile, forensic anthropologist William Rodriguez revealed he planned to testify that the tape’s placement couldn’t be reliably dated due to decomposition and animal disturbance, and that a prosecution video overlaying Caylee’s face onto her skull was misleading. But Rodriguez hadn’t shared these opinions with prosecutors or included them in his official report, prompting Judge Belvin Perry to remove him from the stand temporarily. Perry accused defense attorney Jose Baez of intentional deception, warning of possible contempt charges, yet allowed Rodriguez to return after prosecutors reviewed his findings. The defense continues to argue that Caylee accidentally drowned in the family pool on June 16, 2008, and that her parents concealed the death out of panic — a claim rejected by George Anthony. The trial, now entering its fifth week, remains highly contentious, with both sides battling over forensic interpretation and procedural fairness.

At Eaton House Belgravia School, one of London’s most exclusive pre-preparatory institutions, parents have been asked to avoid feeding their sons any foods containing nuts—including peanut butter or nut-containing cereals—even at home during the school week. The policy, introduced to protect children with severe nut allergies, prohibits not only nut consumption at school but also breakfasts at home that might expose classmates to allergens through scent or residue.

The private school, which educates boys aged four to eight and charges £13,320 per year, also discourages bringing sandwiches or yoghurt to school breaks, citing concerns over messiness in classrooms. Headmistress Miss Lucy Watts explained in her welcome letter: 'Due to some extreme allergies, please do not give your son anything like peanut butter or cereals containing nuts for breakfast during the week, as this can affect boys with allergies.'

While many UK schools ban nuts within school premises, Eaton House has taken a more extensive approach by regulating home meals—a move that has drawn both support and criticism. The Anaphylaxis Campaign, a UK charity supporting those with severe allergies, argues that such strict policies may inadvertently foster a false sense of security, preventing children from learning how to manage real-world exposure.

Scientifically, peanut allergies are indeed among the most common and potentially life-threatening, affecting approximately one in 100 people in the UK. However, research indicates that reactions triggered solely by inhaling peanut aroma are extremely rare, as the allergenic proteins are not typically airborne in sufficient concentrations. According to TeensHealth, the smell of peanut-containing foods does not contain the protein necessary to provoke a reaction.

While most childhood allergies to milk or eggs are outgrown, only about 20% of children with nut allergies lose them over time—meaning four out of five will carry them into adulthood. For some, severity may decrease with age; for others, it may increase.

article_content: Monica Lewis, a 57-year-old grandmother living with epilepsy, died after waiting more than an hour for an ambulance following a life-threatening seizure. Her partner, 73-year-old Harry Smith, dialed 999 at 12:29 a.m. on Friday when she began convulsing violently and cried out, 'I’m going to die.' Despite the severity, the London Ambulance Service initially classified the call as Category C—designed for serious but non-immediately life-threatening situations—with a 19-minute response target. For nearly 47 minutes, two ambulances en route to her Croydon home were diverted to other calls labeled 'higher priority.' At 1:16 a.m., the call was upgraded to Red 2, indicating a life-threatening emergency—but by the time paramedics arrived at 1:39 a.m., Monica had gone into cardiac arrest. Harry, who considered her his wife, stated: 'If the ambulance had come in time, she would have survived. That’s a fact.' Her daughter, Gemma Senior, expressed outrage: 'She lived just ten minutes from the hospital. How did this happen?' Medical professionals emphasize that prolonged seizures, known as status epilepticus, can lead to brain damage or cardiac arrest without rapid intervention. Yet current protocols often fail to recognize this urgency. In light of this tragedy, NHS leaders are considering a controversial policy shift: raising the official response target for Red 2 calls from 8 minutes to 19 minutes—a move critics argue normalizes systemic failure. The case echoes that of Michelle Cooper, a 52-year-old cyclist who died after being discharged from an overwhelmed hospital despite suffering a head injury, underscoring a broader crisis in emergency care capacity.

Donald Trump has withdrawn a lawsuit he recently filed against city officials in Doral, Florida, over noise-ordinance violations at his resort, Trump National Doral — which hosted the Miss Universe pageant last month.

Trump spokesman Ed Russo told the Miami Herald on Thursday that the lawsuit was being dropped in favor of negotiations. 'In good faith, we have decided to voluntarily withdraw our lawsuit against the city, and we look forward to productive discourse regarding this matter,' Russo said.

Records show that since August, Doral’s code-compliance department has issued more than 100 violations to Trump National Doral, primarily for lawn maintenance crews generating 'unreasonably loud noise.'

In the lawsuit filed February 12, Trump argued that the ordinance is 'vague and ambiguous in its definition of prohibited activity' and grants the city’s Code Enforcement Department 'unfettered discretion' in determining violations.

Trump rejected the allegations, stating, 'This is the finest resort in the world, and you have to cut the grass. Why is it that we have brand-new equipment and get fined, when the previous owners never received any citations? Maybe it's because I have money.'

Trump’s lawyers say each violation carries a $1,500 fine and that he has already spent $50,000 in legal fees defending against them. They also state that since purchasing the property out of bankruptcy in 2012, Trump has repeatedly urged the city to revise the noise ordinance.

The resort recently hosted the Miss Universe pageant. Trump expressed uncertainty about whether the dispute might affect the recently announced plan to award him a key to the city of Doral. 'If it does, this is much more important,' he said. 'They may be giving me the key to the city, but I have not been treated right.'

Separately, Trump has filed a $100 million lawsuit against Palm Beach County, alleging that officials have deliberately redirected air traffic over his Mar-a-Lago estate in an act of retaliation. He claims the FAA, under pressure from the county’s airport director — previously named in litigation by Trump — now routes nearly all eastbound flights directly over the historic property.

The lawsuit asserts that noise, vibrations, and emissions from low-flying aircraft are causing structural damage to Mar-a-Lago’s porous stone, Spanish tiles, roofing, floors, and columns, while destroying its once-serene atmosphere. Trump described the actions as 'deliberate and malicious.'
